newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Dlr seen easing vs mark, yen through 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Dlr seen easing vs mark, yen through 1997.

text.p: Profit-taking may sap some of the dollar's recent vigor against the German mark and Japanese yen over the next few months, a Reuters poll showed.
The U.S. unit surged to a 34-month high against the mark at 1.6935 on Wednesday and hit a fresh four-year high at 124.72 versus the yen last week.
But despite the dollar's recent rally, market experts said its strength is likely to wane at some point.

"If you got down to where we were at the beginning of the month, giving back four or five pfennigs, it still would not be catastrophic as far as the technical picture is concerned," said Elliot Dix, assistant vice president at Signet Bank.
"I expect some sort of profit-taking eventually," he said, adding that "we would have expected it prior to this in a larger way than we've seen."
On average, the forecasters said the greenback will inch lower against the mark during the next month to trade at 1.6839 and fall gradually to 1.6450 by year-end.

Similarly, dollar/yen is expected to fall from its current levels to stand at 123.22 in one month's time. It is then expected to decline progressively to about 120.60 by the end of the fourth quarter.
Dix said the retrenchment he expects in the dollar will not be based on economic fundamentals.
"The fundamentals are very positive, it's just the speculative outlook collapsing a little bit," he said.

Sal Guatieri, senior economist at Bank of Montreal in Toronto, said cautious statements made about the dollar's strength at a Group of Seven (G7) meeting last weekend may also put downward pressure on the unit. But he doubts the officials were looking to cap the U.S. dollar's upside potential.
"As long as the fundamentals point to further dollar strength, that's where the market will take it and that's where the G7 officials will allow it go," he said.
Although the dollar is expected to loose some of its strength in the near term, economists said it will not drift too far from its current levels.
Guatieri said that, currently, the dollar/mark rise reflects the "familiar story" of a sluggish German economy.
"In contrast, the U.S. economy is fairly healthy and there is an ongoing diverging risk in (monetary) policies," he said.
The Federal Reserve bank might have to tighten short-term interest rates, while the Bundesbank might have to ease credit, Guatieri added.

In addition, Kathleen Stephansen, international economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp, said the U.S. economy is "considerably stronger than its major counterparts" and it is likely to see the Fed moving to a tighter monetary policy.
"As long as the conviction roams around in the market, the dollar will remain well bid," she said. But she said by year-end "you will see a downward correction."
Additionally, the experts projected sterling will advance moderately against the dollar, after a brief decline, due to an expected tightening of monetary policy in the UK.
The poll showed sterling will decline to about $1.62 one month out, but will advance to $1.73 by the end of the year.
